title: Chapter 13.  The 2019 Reorganisation — Abrogation of Article 370 & Creation of Two Union Territories

blocks.content: This is the pivotal turning-point chapter of the entire book — the single event that separates J&K's 'old status' (Chapters 9-10) from its 'new status' (Chapters 14-16). Every candidate should be able to state precisely what was done, on what dates, through which legal instruments, and what the stated rationale and reactions were on different sides.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: In August 2019, the Parliament passed the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019, bifurcating the state into two Union Territories.
Presidential Order C.O. 272 rendered Article 370 inoperative and superseded the special privileges under Article 35A.
Jammu & Kashmir was reconstituted as a Union Territory with a Legislative Assembly.
Ladakh was constituted as a separate Union Territory without a Legislative Assembly.
The Supreme Court of India unanimously upheld the constitutional validity of the reorganisation in December 2023.

blocks.content: On 5 August 2019, the Government of India took a coordinated set of actions that together are commonly referred to as the 'abrogation of Article 370'. First, the President of India issued the Constitution (Application to Jammu and Kashmir) Order, 2019 (C.O. 272), which superseded the 1954 Presidential Order and effectively extended the entire Constitution of India to J&K, rendering Article 35A automatically inoperative in the process (see Chapter 10).

Simultaneously, a Statutory Resolution was moved and passed in both Houses of Parliament recommending that Article 370 cease to apply — since J&K was under President's Rule at the time (imposed in December 2018 after the collapse of the earlier coalition government), the President's Rule meant that the powers ordinarily exercised by the state's own elected government/legislature for such a recommendation were, per the government's legal position, vested in Parliament and the Governor acting on the Union's behalf, a legal-procedural basis that itself became a central point of later constitutional challenge.

Article 370(1) itself was then used as the mechanism to modify/discontinue its own further application via this process, a legal technique whose validity was subsequently challenged before, and ultimately upheld by, the Supreme Court of India (see below).
The 2019 Reorganisation — Abrogation of Article 370 & Creation of Two Union Territories

On 9 August 2019, Parliament passed the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019, which took effect from 31 October 2019 (deliberately chosen to coincide with the birth anniversary of Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, historically associated with the integration of India's princely states), bifurcating the former state of Jammu and Kashmir into two separate Union Territories: 'Jammu and Kashmir' (with a Legislative Assembly) and 'Ladakh' (without a Legislative Assembly).

cells: Presidential Order (C.O. 272) extends the full Constitution of India to J&K; Parliament's Statutory Resolution recommends Article 370 cease to apply (rendering Article 35A inoperative)
A further Presidential Order formally declares that Article 370's provisions cease to apply, except for Clause (1), which remains as a residual/enabling provision
Parliament passes the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019
Reorganisation Act takes effect — J&K state formally bifurcated into two Union Territories: J&K (with Assembly) and Ladakh (without Assembly)

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: 31 October 2019, the effective date of the bifurcation, was deliberately chosen to coincide with Sardar Patel's birth anniversary — Patel, as India's first Deputy Prime Minister and Home Minister, is historically credited with integrating the vast majority of India's princely states into the Union shortly after Independence, and the government explicitly framed the 2019 reorganisation as completing this integration process.

items: The Government of India's stated justification for the move included: ending what it characterised as J&K's 'separatist' constitutional exceptionalism and fully integrating the region into the Indian Union on the same constitutional footing as other states; enabling direct application of central welfare laws, reservation policies, and economic legislation previously blocked or delayed by the state's separate legal framework; opening the region's land and investment climate to outside capital and residents by removing Article 35A's restrictions; and improving governance and reducing corruption associated, in the government's characterisation, with the earlier system.

The government also argued that Article 370's 'temporary' character (as reflected in its constitutional placement, see Chapter 9) meant its removal was constitutionally permissible and consistent with the Article's own original design, rather than a departure from it.

blocks.content: The move drew sharply divided reactions. It was welcomed by the ruling BJP and its supporters as fulfilling a long-standing party manifesto commitment and as a step toward full national integration and development. It was opposed by most mainstream J&K regional political parties (including the National Conference and the Peoples Democratic Party) and several national opposition parties, who variously characterised it as a unilateral, procedurally improper move that bypassed the spirit (if not, in the government's view, the letter) of the accession-era understanding, and as having been accompanied by an extended security lockdown, communications blackout, and the preventive detention of numerous political leaders (including former Chief Ministers) in the immediate aftermath — restrictions that drew both domestic and international criticism on human-rights and democratic-process grounds, alongside support from those who viewed the security measures as a necessary, temporary precaution against unrest.

Internationally, Pakistan strongly condemned the move and downgraded diplomatic relations with India; China also objected specifically to the inclusion of Ladakh (given its own territorial claims in the region) as a separate Union Territory. The United Nations and most other countries generally treated the move as an internal constitutional matter for India, while continuing to call, in various forums, for the underlying India-Pakistan dispute to be resolved peacefully.

items: Remember that UT of J&K has a Legislative Assembly (similar to Puducherry/Delhi), whereas UT of Ladakh is administered directly without a legislature.
Focus on C.O. 272 and C.O. 273, which modified Article 367 to substitute 'Constituent Assembly' with 'Legislative Assembly'.
Both Union Territories share a common High Court (High Court of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh).

blocks.content: Numerous petitions challenging the constitutional validity of the abrogation were filed before the Supreme Court of India. In its landmark judgment in December 2023 (In Re: Article 370 of the Constitution), a 5-judge Constitution Bench unanimously upheld the constitutional validity of the abrogation of Article 370, holding that the Article was indeed a temporary provision that the President was competent to declare inoperative through the process used, while also directing the Election Commission of India to conduct Assembly elections in the UT of J&K by 30 September 2024 and calling for the restoration of statehood 'at the earliest' — without fixing a specific deadline for the latter.

★ EXAM POINT: The Supreme Court's December 2023 verdict is essential exam material: it UPHELD the abrogation's constitutional validity (a settled legal question as of that judgment), while separately DIRECTING elections by September 2024 (which were duly held, see Chapter 16) and calling for eventual statehood restoration without a fixed timeline (a still-pending political question, discussed in Chapter 29).

items: 5 August 2019: Presidential Order (C.O. 272) + Parliament's Statutory Resolution effectively abrogate Article 370's operative effect; Article 35A rendered inoperative.
9 August 2019: Parliament passes the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019.
31 October 2019 (Sardar Patel's birth anniversary): Act takes effect — bifurcation into J&K UT (with Assembly) and Ladakh UT (without Assembly).

Reactions were sharply divided domestically and internationally; the move was accompanied by an extended security lockdown/communications restrictions and leader detentions in its immediate aftermath.

December 2023 Supreme Court verdict: UPHELD the abrogation's validity; directed Assembly elections in J&K UT by 30 September 2024; called for statehood restoration 'at the earliest' without a fixed deadline.
